summary: One bitstream, two halves, two working groups. Visual volumetric video-based coding is the shared format: it cuts a volumetric frame into patches, projects them onto flat planes, and codes the resulting occupancy, geometry and attribute pictures with an ordinary video codec - AVC, HEVC or VVC - while a small atlas of patch descriptions says how to put the points back in space. Video-based point cloud compression is one application of it, an annex of the same part, owned by the 3D graphics group; MPEG immersive video is the other, a separate part that normatively references the shared format and extends it, owned by the video coding group. The published state is edition 3 of Part 5 in March 2025 and edition 2 of Part 12 in September 2025, with conformance and reference software for the immersive half published in 2026 and the reference encoder public under a BSD licence. What it covers: volumetric video, end to end and seriously - profiles, tiers, six levels, two named conformance points, and a real camera model for multi-camera capture with perspective, equirectangular and orthographic projections. What it leaves to others: everything a world needs. It has no scene graph, no scripting, no identity, no networking session, no anchors and no audio; those rows are honestly out of scope, not missing. Four traps for a standards audience. First, handedness: the frame that patches reconstruct into is described as left-handed, opposite to glTF, OpenUSD and every web runtime on this map, and the block that could name the axis convention is optional and often absent. Second, the standard does not deliver itself - storage in the ISO base media file format and transport over adaptive streaming are Part 10, a different part, so any claim that this format streams is really a claim about its neighbour. Third, meshes: the scope names mesh representations as a target of the generic mechanism, but no mesh coding is published here; that is Part 29, still in development, and the planned fourth edition of Part 5 is what folds it in. Fourth, splats: a first amendment to this part that would add Gaussian splat coding through the same video-based framework has been promoted, and MPEG has an open exploration with a call for content dated July 2026, so the row that reads empty today is the row most likely to change next. One more thing a reader should know: the published text sits behind ISO's paywall, so every quote in this file comes from MPEG's own freely published documents - the 2020 final draft of Part 5, the approved white papers of 2021 and 2026, the standards pages, and the public reference software. Where a fact could have changed between the 2020 draft and the published editions, the note says which document it came from.

coverage.note: A coding standard, not a renderer. It stops at decoding and reconstruction; the immersive video half describes a reference renderer and then says nobody has to follow it.
